entries.text: Thom observes that most of cinema's great sound sequences are point-of-view sequences. Decide early — ideally in the script — whose ears the audience is inside, because that choice dictates what gets heard and what gets filtered away.

source.title: Designing a Movie for Sound

entries.text: A memory transition can ride on sound: Thom describes the rhythmic clank of a mill morphing into the cadence of a train as the story slips back in time.

source.title: Designing a Movie for Sound

entries.text: When the picture is ambiguous — extreme lenses, tilted or moving frames, darkness at the edges — the audience leans on its ears. Thom calls it starving the eye, and urges sound people to lobby for such shots.

source.title: Designing a Movie for Sound

entries.text: When people are talking, they are not listening.

source.title: More Confessions of a Sound Designer

entries.text: In Contact's tunnel ride, giving a panned sound to each of 10–20 similar flying objects would have smeared into pink noise. Thom asked the visual effects team to frame shots so viewers track only one or two objects at a time.

source.title: More Confessions of a Sound Designer

entries.text: A sound only becomes compelling when someone on screen perceives it. If no character reacts, it stays background noise — unless it comes back later in a scene where somebody truly listens.

source.title: More Confessions of a Sound Designer

entries.text: Audience fatigue comes from sustained average level, not peaks. Like a roller coaster that lasts minutes rather than half an hour, an action sequence needs slow stretches between the fast ones so intensity can feel new again.

source.title: Are Movies Getting Too Loud?

entries.text: On Contact, the mixers agreed ahead of time which passages music would lead and which effects would carry. An action scene doesn't need every element peaking at once to land.

source.title: On Being Creative

entries.text: Before shooting, handle every object and surface on the set and listen for dramatic potential. A table shoved across the floor might carry more menace than the click of a cocked gun.

source.title: On Being Creative

entries.text: In Forrest Gump's Vietnam battle, mortars begin far off and creep closer and harder, conveying distance without reverse shots; the low, ground-level camera justified bullets whipping right past the audience's ears.

source.title: A Few Notes on Forrest Gump

entries.text: Contact opens by pulling back through space past ever-older broadcasts; after the earliest one there's static, then roughly 45 seconds of true silence that the team refused to paper over with music.

entries.text: For Contact's dreamlike beach scene, only one sound plays at a time — lapping waves, wind in palms, her father scooping sand — with no music or dialogue, keeping the moment deliberately artificial.

source.title: Making Contact

entries.text: In What Lies Beneath's near-drowning, once Claire's ears go under everything is muffled, then bubbles and nearly musical tones are layered on with no conventional score, as if you are inside her head underwater.

source.title: Randy Thom, Sound Designer, 'What Lies Beneath'

entries.text: The ghostly whispers in What Lies Beneath mix the actresses with recordings of older women praying, chopped up and reversed so no word is intelligible — leaving it unclear whether Claire hears something real.

source.title: Randy Thom Looks Back on 40 Years with Skywalker Sound

entries.text: Thom and Burtt recorded gunshots, explosions and nature at Skywalker Ranch before its buildings existed. In the field you stumble on unexpected sounds, and those surprises often connect to a story's themes.

entries.text: Hearing a hand-cranked generator in an old John Wayne movie, Burtt bought a WWII generator on eBay and performed it in the studio, shaping its soft whir to WALL·E's slow movements.

entries.text: For WALL·E, Burtt cut sound-and-picture 'character studies' like audition tapes; animators then animated to them and sound and animation were refined back and forth, which made the robot feel more authentic.

source.title: Locarno 2024 Interview: Hollywood Legend Ben Burtt on Inventing Ewok Language, Finding E.T., NASA Documentaries

entries.text: Rather than garbling English, the Ewok language grew from recordings of an elderly woman telling stories in a rarely heard language; actors then imitated her. The same approach later fed Jawas, Hutts and Gungans.

source.title: Locarno 2024 Interview: Hollywood Legend Ben Burtt on Inventing Ewok Language, Finding E.T., NASA Documentaries

entries.text: E.T.'s voice came from a retired, heavy-smoking woman Burtt met by chance outside a camera store. Spielberg judged her through blind temp-cut tests, and 'E.T. phone home' took around 200 takes to yield two or three keepers.

source.title: Star Wars sound (Burtt quotes from Film Sound Today)

entries.text: The Imperial Walkers' stomp is a machinist's punch press, modified and layered with bicycle chains dropped onto concrete — mechanical heft plus rattling detail.

source.title: Star Wars sound (Burtt quotes from Film Sound Today)

entries.text: Luke's landspeeder whoosh is Los Angeles Harbor Freeway traffic recorded through a vacuum-cleaner pipe — the tube acting as a resonant filter that turns ordinary road roar into something futuristic.

entries.text: For The Empire Strikes Back, Burtt recorded howitzer rounds at a New Mexico artillery base — their shrieking shells became Star Destroyer launches — and paired P-38 fighters passing at 400 mph with Hoover Dam's spillway for a giant blast.

source.title: Do you know what Wookiees sound like?

entries.text: To make a lightsaber move, Burtt played its hum loop through a speaker and swung a microphone past it, capturing a natural Doppler pitch shift for every sweep and swing.

entries.text: The TIE fighter howl starts with a car passing a mic on wet pavement, layered with elephant calls pulled from an old Fox library — a mundane pass-by made terrifying by an animal scream.

source.title: Star Wars: Pew Pew!

entries.text: Chewbacca began as hours of recordings of a pet bear. Burtt sorted the clips by emotion — angry, cute, questioning — then slowed and manipulated them into a 'word list' he could edit into performances.

source.title: Star Wars: Pew Pew!

entries.text: R2-D2 blends human and machine: Burtt whistled and vocalized while playing an ARP synthesizer, so the electronic beeps carry the inflection of a real performance.

source.title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day sound

entries.text: The T-1000's liquid-metal morph: Dust-Off sprayed into a flour-and-water mix, recorded with a condom-sheathed mic, gave metallic, evolving bubbles. A violin bow on metal had been tried first and rejected as too ethereal.

source.title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day sound

entries.text: The T-1000 oozing through steel bars is dog food slowly sucked out of a can; bullets splatting into it are an upturned glass slammed into a bucket of yogurt for a hard edge on the goop.

source.title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day sound

entries.text: You would get the deep thud with a high ring-out.

source.title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day sound

entries.text: T2 sets up its biggest hits with removal: silence and a detonator click before the Cyberdyne blast, ambience dropping out before the steel-mill gunshot, engine and music cutting during the Harley's flight until it lands.

entries.text: But there was no bigger candy store for sound design than Jurassic Park.

source.title: Jurassic Bark: How Sound Design Changed Our Imaginations

entries.text: The T. rex roar rests on a low, tiger-like base topped by a baby elephant's scream. The elephant made that sound only once, so the single recording was reused for every roar in the film.

source.title: Jurassic Bark: How Sound Design Changed Our Imaginations

entries.text: Some of Jurassic Park's most menacing calls had unglamorous origins: raptor barks from mating tortoises plus hissing geese, the Gallimimus herd from horses in estrus, and Rydstrom's own Jack Russell terrier in the T. rex.

source.title: The Raptor Noises in Jurassic Park Are Mating Tortoises

entries.text: West Side Story opens on demolition, and the sound keeps it going off screen: the neighborhood is audibly being torn down in later scenes, so the film never has to show it again.

source.title: 189: Gary Rydstrom

entries.text: In West Side Story's knife fight, the blade swishes were kept high and sharp while the ambience stayed low beneath them — like a band arranger clearing space for a featured instrument.

source.title: 189: Gary Rydstrom

entries.text: To get from the rumble's deaths to the upbeat 'I Feel Pretty', the team stripped away natural sound and left only church bells, giving the audience a moment to absorb the loss.

entries.text: For Saving Private Ryan's tanks, Spielberg wanted odd sounds bouncing between buildings. Rydstrom put scraping metal and engines on quarter-inch tape and rocked the reels by hand, scratch-style, for strange rhythmic squeals.

source.title: Gary Rydstrom interview (Mix, February 2004)

entries.text: To give Luxo Jr.'s lamps character, Rydstrom recorded everyday objects — unscrewing a bulb, scraping metal — and kept only the sounds that happened to feel sad or gleeful.

source.title: The Sound of Saving Private Ryan

entries.text: Saving Private Ryan's battle sounds came from real WWII weapons, with impacts edited by hand. Veterans Rydstrom consulted could identify guns by ear, like the M1 rifle's telltale cartridge ping.
